prose.def: To imitate someone or something, following their example in behavior or character.
prose.article: Μιμέομαι means to imitate or copy, taking another person or their conduct as your model. The New Testament's four uses split between imitating a person (as in 2 Thessalonians 3:7 and Hebrews 13:7) and imitating what is done (3 John 1:11, "imitate what is good"), but both are really the same basic idea of following an example. prose.def: A paid worker hired for wages, contrasted with a slave who serves without pay.

prose.def: An adverb meaning barely, with difficulty, or scarcely — something that happens only through great effort or hardship.
prose.article: μόλις is an adverb meaning that something is done only with difficulty or barely accomplished. prose.def: A young man, typically someone in the prime of life (anywhere up to about forty years old).
prose.article: Νεανίας simply means a young man — a male in his youth or prime, which ancient usage could stretch as old as about forty. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 5 times, all in Acts, and translators render it consistently as "young man" (the apparent variety in the measured senses is just phrasing differences around the same idea). prose.def: Neapolis, a coastal city of Macedonia that served as a seaport on Paul's journey.
prose.article: Neapolis is a place name, not an ordinary word: it marks a maritime city in Macedonia where Paul's ship landed. The name literally combines the Greek words for "new" (νέος) and "city" (πόλις), so it simply means "new town" — and Abbott-Smith notes the form was often written as two words, Νέα Πόλις. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Acts 16:11, and Moulton-Milligan shows the word turning up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions as well.

prose.def: Describing a person, body, or thing that is no longer alive; also used figuratively for what is lifeless or powerless.
prose.article: νεκρός means "dead" in the plainest sense, and that is how it reads in 125 of its 131 Byzantine occurrences (98%). It works both as an adjective ("dead, lifeless") and as a noun ("the dead," a corpse), and the New Testament stretches it figuratively too — for people spiritually dead, or for things like faith and works that are powerless and inoperative. The everyday papyri reinforce its literal weight: documents list "expenses for the corpse" and note that a dead body was widely regarded as unclean, as in a Torino papyrus stating that certain goddesses abhor dead bodies.

prose.def: To put to death or make as good as dead, used both literally and figuratively for deadening something within a person.
prose.article: This verb means to make dead or put to death, and the New Testament uses it both literally and figuratively across its 3 occurrences. It can describe a body so worn by age that it is as good as dead, or it can be a command to kill off carnal impulses, as in Colossians 3:5. A striking parallel comes from an ancient inscription where a tomb pleads, "O man, pass not by my body, now a corpse," using this same word for a literal dead body.

prose.def: The condition or process of being dead, deadening, or lifelessness, whether of the body or its parts.
prose.article: νέκρωσις describes deadness or the process of dying — either an active putting to death or a lifeless, deadened condition. It appears only twice in the New Testament: in Romans 4:19 it refers to the lifelessness of Sarah's womb (the digest's odd 'hundred' label reflects a measurement glitch, since the sense there is barrenness or deadness), and in 2 Corinthians 4:10 it means the dying or death that Paul carries in his body. A striking parallel from the papyri-era sources, cited by Deissmann, uses the word for seeds that 'come to life again after death and destruction by decay,' showing its everyday range covered natural deadness as well as deliberate killing.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences and a misfiring 'hundred' label on the Romans verse, the measured data is thin and partly unreliable, though the lexica agree on the core meaning.
